**Editor’s Note: USC students partner with Hubli community to tackle drinking water quality**

**Hubli, India** — In S.M. Krishna Nagar, a residential community in Hubli, access to drinking water is part of daily life — and daily concern. For many families, water may arrive intermittently, be stored in household containers, or pass through aging local infrastructure before it reaches a glass. Even when water looks clear, residents can still worry about contamination that is invisible to the eye.

This summer, the **University of Southern California Hubli Water and Health Team** is working alongside local residents, community leaders and health partners to better understand those concerns — and to help improve the quality and safety of drinking water in the neighborhood.

The project focuses on a central public health question: **How can a community identify risks in its drinking water system and take practical steps to reduce them?**

Over the course of the summer, the USC team is expected to study how water is collected, transported, stored and consumed in S.M. Krishna Nagar. Their work may include household surveys, water-quality testing, mapping of water sources, interviews with residents and observation of sanitation and storage practices. By combining scientific analysis with community input, the team aims to identify where contamination risks may be entering the system — whether at the source, during distribution, or inside homes.

But the effort is not only technical. It is also deeply human.

Clean water is tied to school attendance, childhood health, medical expenses and the everyday dignity of families. Contaminated drinking water can contribute to gastrointestinal illness and other preventable health problems, especially among children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems. In communities where water access is inconsistent, residents often rely on storage tanks, containers or backup sources — each of which can introduce new vulnerabilities.

The USC Hubli Water and Health Team’s summer project is designed to support solutions that are realistic for the local context. That could mean recommending safer household storage practices, identifying areas where infrastructure needs attention, supporting community education around water handling, or helping local stakeholders prioritize future interventions.

The team’s work in S.M. Krishna Nagar reflects a broader model of global health collaboration: universities can bring research tools and technical training, but lasting progress depends on partnership with the people who live the challenge every day.

As the summer unfolds, the USC students and faculty involved in the project will continue gathering data, listening to residents and working toward recommendations that can help make drinking water safer in S.M. Krishna Nagar.

In a neighborhood where water is essential to every meal, every school day and every household routine, even small improvements can have a lasting impact.

# USC Students Take on Water Purification Challenges in India

Access to clean water is one of the most urgent public health issues in the world, and for many communities in India, it remains a daily challenge. This summer, a team of University of Southern California students traveled to India to work alongside local residents, educators, and health partners on water purification solutions designed not only to improve water quality, but also to support long-term community education.

According to the World Health Organization, diarrhoeal disease is a major global health threat, especially for children. WHO estimates that there are nearly **1.7 billion cases of childhood diarrhoeal disease each year**, and diarrhoeal disease remains one of the leading causes of death among children under five worldwide. Many of these illnesses are linked to unsafe drinking water, inadequate sanitation, and poor hygiene conditions.

For the USC team, those statistics are more than numbers. They represent a call to action.

## Understanding the Local Water Challenges

In the communities the students visited, water contamination can come from several sources. Some households rely on wells, hand pumps, or shared water points that may be vulnerable to bacteria, agricultural runoff, or sewage contamination. In some areas, aging pipes, open drainage systems, and seasonal flooding can increase the risk of polluted water entering everyday water supplies.

Residents also face practical barriers. Even when purification methods are available, they may be too expensive, difficult to maintain, or poorly matched to local needs. A filter that works well in a laboratory may fail in a rural household if replacement parts are unavailable or if families are not trained to use and clean it properly.

That is why the USC students are focusing on more than technology alone.

## A Community-Centered Approach

The team’s project combines water testing, purification research, and public health education. Students are working to identify contaminants of concern, evaluate low-cost purification options, and better understand how families store and use water at home.

Rather than arriving with a one-size-fits-all solution, the team is collaborating with community members to learn what is realistic and sustainable. Their goal is to support water purification systems that are affordable, easy to maintain, and culturally appropriate.

Possible strategies include household filtration, safe water storage practices, boiling or solar disinfection education, and simple testing tools that help families monitor water quality. The students are also studying how education can make these interventions more effective.

## Building Sustainable Education

A major part of the team’s plan is community education that continues after the students leave. To make that possible, they are developing materials that can be shared through schools, local health workers, and community leaders.

Their education plan focuses on practical, repeatable lessons, including:

- How contaminated water can spread disease  
- Why safe water storage matters  
- How to properly use and maintain purification tools  
- When water should be boiled or treated  
- How handwashing and sanitation reduce diarrheal illness  
- How children can help bring health information back to their families  

The students hope to train local partners who can continue teaching these practices year-round. By using a “train-the-trainer” model, the project aims to create a ripple effect: students teach community leaders, community leaders teach families, and families pass habits on to the next generation.

## More Than a Short-Term Project

The USC team recognizes that sustainable change requires trust, local leadership, and long-term commitment. Water purification is not only an engineering problem; it is also a public health, education, and equity issue.

By combining scientific testing with community partnership, the students hope their work can help reduce preventable waterborne illness and support healthier futures. Their experience in India is a reminder that global health solutions are strongest when they are built with communities, not simply for them.

Clean water saves lives. With education, collaboration, and sustainable planning, projects like this can help make safe drinking water a reality for more families.

---

**USC students bring low-cost clean water technology to an underserved community in India**

**HUBLI, India —** In a narrow lane on the edge of Hubli, a city in the southern Indian state of Karnataka, water is more than a daily necessity. It is a daily uncertainty.

For families in one underserved slum community, access to safe drinking water can depend on erratic supply, aging infrastructure and the cost of purification methods many households cannot afford. Now, a six-student team from the University of Southern California is working with local partners to test whether affordable, easy-to-maintain water purification systems can help close that gap.

The USC Water and Health Team traveled to Hubli as part of a pilot project focused on household-level and community-based purification solutions. Their goal: identify systems that are not only effective in removing contaminants, but also practical for families living with limited space, income and reliable utilities.

“We’re not here to drop off technology and leave,” one team member said. “We’re here to understand what people actually need, what they will use, and what can be sustained after we’re gone.”

Over several days, the students met with residents, surveyed water-use habits and tested purification prototypes designed to be low-cost and simple to operate. The systems being piloted are intended to reduce dependence on boiling water or purchasing bottled water — options that can be expensive, time-consuming or inconsistent for low-income households.

In communities like this one, the burden of unsafe water often falls hardest on children, older adults and women, who are frequently responsible for collecting, storing and managing household water. Contaminated water can contribute to gastrointestinal illness and other health problems, creating cycles of missed school, lost wages and added medical expenses.

The students say the technical challenge is only part of the work. A purification system may perform well in a lab, but fail in the field if it is too slow, too costly, difficult to clean or culturally unfamiliar.

That is why the team’s pilot emphasizes feedback from residents. How does the water taste? How long does filtration take? Can the device be repaired locally? Would families trust it enough to use it every day?

Local community organizers helped introduce the USC students to households and guided conversations around water access, sanitation and health concerns. Their involvement, students said, is essential to ensuring the project responds to local realities rather than outside assumptions.

The pilot also reflects a growing trend in global health and engineering education: student teams working across disciplines to develop solutions for communities facing environmental health challenges. For the USC Water and Health Team, the Hubli project sits at the intersection of engineering, public health and social impact.

Still, the students acknowledge that a small pilot is not a cure-all. Clean water access is tied to broader issues, including municipal infrastructure, poverty, housing conditions and public investment. But they hope their work can offer one piece of a larger solution — especially if the systems prove affordable, durable and acceptable to residents.

The next phase will involve analyzing water-quality data, evaluating household feedback and refining the purification designs. If the pilot is successful, the team hopes the model could be expanded to serve more families in Hubli and potentially other communities facing similar challenges.

For residents, the promise is simple: water that is safer to drink, without placing another heavy cost on families already stretching every rupee.

For the students, the lesson is just as clear.

“In the classroom, water is a science problem,” another team member said. “Here, it’s a human problem. And that changes everything.”

---

## USC Students in Hubli Launch Humanitarian Project to Improve Water Safety and Health Awareness

Students from USC in Hubli are undertaking a humanitarian initiative aimed at addressing one of the most urgent public health challenges facing many communities: access to safe drinking water. The project focuses on collecting household-level health and water-access data, supporting families with subsidized water purification technology, and building awareness about the risks associated with contaminated water.

### Understanding the Community’s Water Challenges

The first phase of the project will involve a structured household survey across selected neighborhoods in and around Hubli. Student volunteers will visit homes to collect data on water sources, water storage practices, access to sanitation, frequency of waterborne illnesses, and the financial burden families face when seeking clean water or medical treatment.

The data collection process is designed to help identify the households most vulnerable to unsafe drinking water. Families relying on untreated borewell water, irregular municipal supply, open storage containers, or expensive private water sources will be prioritized. The survey will also document common health concerns such as diarrhea, stomach infections, skin conditions, and other symptoms often linked to contaminated water.

By gathering reliable community-level information, the students hope to move beyond assumptions and design interventions based on real needs.

### Subsidizing Water Purification Technology

Following the assessment, the project will help eligible households access affordable water purification solutions. Many families understand the importance of clean drinking water but are unable to purchase filters or purification devices due to cost barriers. To address this, the USC student team will work with local partners, donors, and technology providers to subsidize purification systems for low-income households.

The selected technology may include household water filters, gravity-based purifiers, or other low-maintenance systems suitable for local conditions. The goal is to ensure that the solution is not only effective but also affordable, easy to use, and sustainable over time.

Families receiving subsidized purification devices will be given basic training on installation, cleaning, maintenance, and safe storage of drinking water. This is essential because even treated water can become contaminated if stored in unhygienic containers or handled improperly.

### Raising Awareness About Contaminated Water Risks

Technology alone cannot solve the problem of unsafe drinking water. A major component of the project is community education. USC students will organize awareness sessions in residential areas, schools, community centers, and local gathering spaces to explain the health risks of contaminated water and the importance of safe water practices.

The awareness campaign will focus on practical topics, including:

- How contaminated water spreads disease  
- Common symptoms of waterborne infections  
- Safe water storage and handling methods  
- The importance of boiling, filtering, or otherwise treating drinking water  
- Cleaning household water containers regularly  
- Handwashing and hygiene practices  
- When to seek medical care for water-related illness  

The students will use simple language, posters, demonstrations, and community discussions to ensure that information is accessible to people of different age groups and literacy levels. They will also engage local leaders, teachers, health workers, and women’s groups to help sustain the message after the initial campaign.

### A Data-Driven and Community-Centered Approach

What makes this project significant is its combination of data, technology, and education. The student team is not simply distributing filters; it is first identifying need, then providing targeted support, and finally ensuring that households understand how to protect themselves from future risk.

The collected data will also help create a clearer picture of water insecurity in the area. It may be used to inform future partnerships with civic authorities, health organizations, and NGOs working on water, sanitation, and public health.

### Expected Impact

Through this initiative, USC students in Hubli aim to reduce exposure to contaminated drinking water, lower the risk of waterborne illnesses, and improve household awareness of safe water practices. The project is expected to benefit families who are most affected by poor water quality and limited access to affordable purification options.

Beyond the immediate health benefits, the initiative will also empower students to become active contributors to community welfare. By working directly with households, listening to residents, and supporting practical solutions, the students are helping build a model of youth-led humanitarian action rooted in compassion, evidence, and local engagement.

### Conclusion

Access to safe drinking water is a basic human need, yet many families continue to face daily uncertainty about the quality of the water they consume. The USC student project in Hubli represents a meaningful step toward addressing this challenge. By collecting household data, subsidizing purification technology, and spreading awareness about contaminated water risks, the initiative seeks to create lasting improvements in health, dignity, and quality of life for vulnerable communities.
